opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think norms against outright lying are really valuable. They're one of the main things that make it possible for a reader to trust a publication at all: if you know a reporter won't just fabricate a quote or invent a statistic, that sets a floor on how wrong you can be by reading them. But that floor is a lot lower than people tend to assume, because there's an enormous amount of room to mislead without ever saying anything literally false.

The most obvious tool is selection. Out of all the true facts available, which ones do you put in the story? Which experts do you call? If you want to make a technology look dangerous, you can find a credible person who'll say it's dangerous, quote them accurately, and you've told no lies. Do the same in the other direction and you get the opposite impression. Each individual sentence survives a fact-check, but the overall picture a reader walks away with can be badly off from what a careful look at the full evidence would support.

Then there's framing and emphasis. What goes in the headline versus paragraph fourteen? Is a risk reported as relative or absolute? "Doubles your risk" and "raises it from one in a million to two in a million" are both true, but they produce very different beliefs. And there's the choice of what counts as news at all. Dramatic, unusual events get covered, and slow trends that matter far more, like steady declines in poverty or gradual improvements in some technology, mostly don't. So even a perfectly honest outlet can leave its audience with systematically distorted beliefs about base rates and about which direction things are going.

A related issue is false balance. Presenting "both sides" sounds fair and doesn't involve lying, but if the evidence is ninety-five to five, treating it as fifty-fifty misinforms people about the state of knowledge.

So I'd say the anti-lying norm is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. What you'd really want is accountability for the accuracy of the impression created, not just the literal truth of the statements. That's much harder to enforce, because it requires judgment about what an ideal summary of the evidence would look like. One thing I find appealing here is track records and forecasting: if outlets or pundits made explicit probabilistic claims and we scored them over time, you'd get feedback on whether readers end up with calibrated beliefs. That catches misleading-but-technically-true coverage that the lying norm misses entirely.

As a reader, the practical upshot is to treat a lack of falsehoods as the minimum. Ask what's been left out, what the base rates are, and whether the sources quoted are representative of expert opinion or were chosen to tell a particular story.

r001.rationale: It says avoiding fabrication helps readers trust a publication, but does not explain that even misinformation-prone media have incentives to avoid it because fabrication is easy to check.

r002.rationale: It explains that choosing and framing individually true facts can create a misleading overall impression and leave readers with false beliefs.

r003.rationale: It discusses selective sourcing in general, but does not mention amplifying a group's misconduct or the resulting hatred when misconduct rates are comparable across groups.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that the norm against outright fabrication in journalism is quite strong and quite valuable. If a reporter at a major outlet is caught inventing quotes or making up events, that's typically career-ending. So on the narrow question of "will this story contain statements the author knows to be false," the norm does a lot of work, and I don't want to understate that.

But the limits show up as soon as you move from "not saying false things" to "leaving the reader with an accurate picture of the world," because those are very different targets. There are a few mechanisms I'd point to.

The most important is selection. A journalist can write a piece where every individual sentence is true and well-sourced, and yet the overall impression is badly misleading, simply by choosing which true things to include and which to leave out, which experts to quote, which anecdotes to lead with. Nothing in the norm against lying touches that. And selection isn't even necessarily conscious; it emerges from what the journalist finds interesting, what their editors think will get clicks, what the readership already believes.

A second mechanism is the use of attribution as a shield. "Critics say," "experts warn," "some have argued." You can convey a claim you'd never be willing to assert in your own voice by finding someone who will assert it and quoting them. The quote is accurate, so you haven't lied. But you've chosen to amplify that particular voice, and the reader comes away believing something that may not be the balance of evidence.

Third, there's a real asymmetry between the incentives on errors of omission versus errors of commission. If you print a false statement, there's a correction mechanism, a reputational cost, sometimes legal exposure. If you simply fail to report something important, or fail to give it the weight it deserves, nobody files a correction. So the system is tuned to catch one kind of failure and essentially blind to the other.

And then there's the question of what happens with uncertain or probabilistic matters, which is where I think the norms really break down. Journalism as a genre is uncomfortable with "we don't know" or "this is maybe 30% likely." The format pushes towards narratives, towards someone being right and someone being wrong. So on exactly the questions where accurate public understanding would most benefit from calibrated uncertainty, like early stages of a pandemic, or forecasting technological developments, the norms don't give you much.

I'd also note that the norm against lying applies to the journalist, not to the sources. A great deal of what appears in news is officials or interested parties making statements that are, let's say, strategically framed. The journalist can accurately report that the statement was made. Whether to flag it as misleading depends on editorial judgment and on whether the outlet is willing to bear the cost of annoying the source.

So my overall view is that the anti-lying norm is a necessary floor, and I'm glad it exists, but it's a pretty low floor relative to what you'd want. If you actually care about whether the public ends up with accurate beliefs, you'd want something closer to the norms you see in, say, good forecasting communities, where you're scored on the accuracy of your overall picture rather than just on avoiding assertions you know to be false. And there are reasons that's hard to implement in journalism, around speed, commercial pressures, and the lack of resolution for most claims. But I think it's worth being clear-eyed that the existing norm is solving a narrower problem than people often assume.

r001.rationale: It says fabrication is career-ending when caught, but does not explain that even misinformation-prone media avoid it because it is easy to check.

r002.rationale: It explains that selecting and arranging individually true statements can leave readers with a misleading overall impression.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss selectively amplifying a group's misconduct, comparisons of misconduct rates across groups, or stoking hatred.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the norm against lying does some real work, but it’s much weaker than a norm of giving your audience an accurate picture of the world. You can say only true things and still leave people with a very misleading impression, because you control which true things they hear.

Suppose you have a very large country, with hundreds of millions of people. There will be examples of almost any kind of outrageous behaviour you might want to highlight. And so you can select a succession of real incidents that makes some problem look pervasive or rapidly worsening, even if its actual frequency is low or declining. Every individual story can be accurately reported, while the overall impression is wrong.

And that’s especially difficult because selection is unavoidable. You can’t report everything. So whereas a fabricated quotation is a fairly clear violation that other journalists can identify and sanction, it’s much harder to enforce a rule about whether your selection of stories is representative. Representative of what? What counts as newsworthy? There’s a lot of room for people’s political preferences, or their audience’s preferences, to determine the answer.

There’s also the distinction between accurately reporting that somebody made a claim and establishing whether the claim is true. You can quote someone saying something false, quote an opponent disagreeing, and have met a certain procedural standard without helping the reader very much in figuring out what actually happened.

So I’d want to ask questions like: What’s the denominator? How common is this? What’s the trend over time? What evidence would point in the other direction? The prohibition on lying is valuable, but it doesn’t by itself produce those habits. And if the incentive is to attract attention or affirm your audience’s worldview, there’s enormous scope to mislead without ever crossing that particular line.

r001.rationale: The response says fabricated quotations are clear violations that other journalists can identify and sanction, explaining why outright fabrication is easier to detect and carries consequences.

r002.rationale: It explains that selecting a succession of true incidents can create a misleading overall impression, even when each report is accurate.

r003.rationale: It discusses making a problem seem pervasive despite low or declining frequency, but does not describe stoking hatred toward a group or compare that group's misconduct rate with others.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, there’s a big gap between not saying anything false and giving people an accurate picture of what’s going on. You can select only true statements and still leave your audience with a very misleading impression, through which stories you cover, which comparisons you make, and which facts you leave out.

Suppose you’re covering some danger, and you report individual instances of it happening. Every story might be completely accurate. But if you increase the amount of coverage tenfold while the underlying danger is actually declining, your readers may become much more worried precisely when they should be becoming less worried. A norm against fabricating incidents doesn’t address that. You need denominators, trends, and some sense of how the risk compares with other risks.

And that’s harder to enforce than a prohibition on lying. You can point to a particular sentence and establish that it’s false. It’s much harder to establish that an editor should have run a different collection of stories. There’s inevitably selection, because you can’t report everything.

So I think the norm against lying is valuable, but it’s a fairly minimal condition. The more demanding standard is: are you helping your audience form more accurate beliefs? If you know that a collection of individually defensible statements is predictably giving people the wrong impression, then checking each sentence for literal truth isn’t enough.

r001.rationale: The response says false sentences are easier to identify than misleading story selection, but does not explain that even misinformation-prone media have incentives to avoid fabrication because it is easy to check.

r002.rationale: It explains that individually true statements can create a misleading impression through story selection, comparisons, and omitted facts.

r003.rationale: It discusses coverage making people misjudge a danger, but does not address selectively amplifying a group’s misconduct, hatred toward that group, or comparisons of misconduct rates across groups.
